title: Meghalaya — more places

places.name: Dawki
places.summary: A border town on the glass-clear Umngot river, 70 km from Shillong — boating, camping at Shnongpdeng and a 1932 suspension bridge.
places.seoTitle: Dawki and the Umngot river, Meghalaya
places.seoDescription: Dawki on the clear Umngot river: boating and camping at Shnongpdeng, the 1932 Dawki Bridge and the Bangladesh border, 70 km from Shillong.

images.alt: Boats on the clear Umngot river below Dawki Bridge
images.caption: Dawki Bridge and the Umngot

overview.text:
Dawki is a small town at the foot of the Jaintia Hills, on the India–Bangladesh border, and it is famous for one thing: the Umngot river, whose water is so clear that the boats on it seem to float above the riverbed. The river marks the border here, and Dawki–Tamabil is one of the few road crossings into Bangladesh, with Sylhet 55 km beyond.

The Dawki Bridge, a suspension bridge built by the British in 1932, spans the river and gives the classic view down onto the boats. Upstream, Shnongpdeng is the place to camp and take a boat out, and the Umngot's rapids also draw people for rafting and kayaking. Dawki is about 70 km from Shillong: shared transport leaves Iewduh market each morning, and buses also make the trip.

items.body: Take a boat out on the clear Umngot.
Camp by the river at Shnongpdeng.
Raft or kayak the Umngot's rapids.
Walk to the 1932 Dawki suspension bridge.

how_to_reach.text: Shared transport leaves Iewduh in Shillong for Dawki every morning, and buses also cover the 70 km journey.

places.name: Jowai
places.summary: The Pnar heartland of the Jaintia Hills, 64 km from Shillong — base for Krang Suri falls, Thadlaskein Lake and the Nartiang monoliths.
places.seoTitle: Jowai, Jaintia Hills — waterfalls, monoliths and the Pnar
places.seoDescription: Jowai, 64 km from Shillong: base for Krang Suri and Tyrshi falls, Thadlaskein Lake, Nartiang's monoliths and the Behdienkhlam festival in July.

overview.text:
Jowai is the headquarters of West Jaintia Hills and the home of the Pnar people, a Khasi sub-tribe. The town sits at 1,365 m on a plateau wrapped on three sides by the Myntdu river, and it is quieter and less touristy than Shillong or Sohra.

Most of what brings visitors is just outside town: the turquoise pools of Krang Suri and Tyrshi waterfalls, Thadlaskein Lake, Ialong eco-park above the Pynthorwah valley, and the great standing stones of Nartiang. In town, wander Iaw Musiang, one of the district's oldest markets, and see Jowai Presbyterian Church, the oldest church in the Jaintia Hills, built by the Welsh mission in the late 19th century. Come in July for Behdienkhlam, the Jaintia Hills' big festival.

how_to_reach.text: Jowai is 64 km from Shillong on NH 44. There is no rail or air link; the nearest railway is at Guwahati, about 160 km away.

local_transport.text: Shared Tata Sumos and Indicas are the main way around the district, with good availability through the day.

items.body: Swim in the pool below Krang Suri falls.
Watch the sunset over the Pynthorwah valley at Ialong eco-park.

best_time.text: Come in July for Behdienkhlam, the traditional festival of the Jaintia Hills.

places.name: Krang Suri Falls
places.summary: A blue-water curtain fall over a cave, half an hour from Jowai, with a swimming pool below (life jackets on hire).
places.seoDescription: Krang Suri (Krangshuri) Falls, half an hour from Jowai: a curtain of water over a cave into a clear blue pool; swim with a hired life jacket.

images.alt: Krang Suri Falls dropping into a blue pool
images.caption: Krang Suri Falls

overview.text:
Krang Suri is a waterfall in the Jaintia Hills, about half an hour's drive from Jowai. It doesn't plunge off a cliff like the falls around Sohra. Instead, a calm river suddenly drops as a wide curtain of water over a cave, into a pool of startlingly clear blue water set deep in the forest.

A pleasant path leads down to it, and the water seems to get bluer the closer you get. You can swim in the pool — life jackets are rented at the site, and you should wear one. Combine it with Nartiang's monoliths for a day out from Jowai.

items.title: Swimming
items.body: Allowed with a hired life jacket
Walk down the forest path to the falls.
Swim in the clear blue pool with a hired life jacket.
Look for the cave behind the curtain of water.

places.name: Nartiang Monoliths
places.summary: A garden of Jaintia royal monoliths from 1500–1835, the tallest about 8 m, in the old summer capital of Nartiang.
places.seoDescription: Nartiang's garden of monoliths: menhirs and dolmens raised by the Jaintia kings between 1500 and 1835, the tallest about 8 m, near Jowai.

images.alt: Standing stones under trees at Nartiang
images.caption: Nartiang monoliths

overview.text:
Nartiang was the summer capital of the Jaintia kings of Sutnga in the 17th century, and its garden of monoliths is one of the most striking sights in Meghalaya. A large collection of stones stands in a hillside garden, raised as memorials to kings, legendary figures and victories between about 1500 and 1835.

The upright stones, or menhirs, honour male ancestors; the flat table-stones, the dolmens, honour women. The tallest menhir stands about 8 metres high, and walking among them you get a sense of the strength it took to raise them. Cross to the far side of the garden for views of village life. The 500-year-old Nartiang Durga Temple is about 3 km away, and Krang Suri falls makes a good pairing on a day trip from Jowai.

places.name: Nartiang Durga Temple
places.summary: A 600-year-old Shakta pitha of the Jaintia kings, where Durga is worshipped in a Khasi way, as a plantain trunk.
places.seoDescription: Nartiang Durga Temple: a 600-year-old Shakta pitha near Jowai where Durga is worshipped as a plantain trunk, with a four-day Durga Puja.

images.alt: The old stone at the Nartiang Durga Temple
images.caption: Nartiang Durga Temple

overview.text:
The Nartiang Durga Temple is about 600 years old and one of the 51 Shakta pithas, the holiest shrines of the goddess. It was built by the Jaintia kings, who made Nartiang their summer capital, and it blends Hindu worship with older Khasi tradition.

In keeping with the Khasi custom of not using images of gods, Durga is represented here by a plantain trunk decked with marigolds rather than an idol. Durga Puja is the temple's great festival: over four days the decorated plant is worshipped, and at the end it is carried down and immersed in the Myntdu river. Within walking distance, a small Shiva temple still holds the remains of old cannons — a sign the site was once part of a fort. Combine it with the monoliths, about 3 km away.

places.name: Mawsynram
places.summary: The rain capital of India, 69 km from Shillong — reportedly the wettest place on Earth.
places.seoTitle: Mawsynram — the wettest place on Earth?
places.seoDescription: Mawsynram, 69 km from Shillong and 15 km west of Cherrapunji, averages 11,872 mm of rain a year — reportedly the wettest place on Earth.

images.alt: Green hills and cloud at Mawsynram
images.caption: Mawsynram

overview.text:
Mawsynram is a small town in the East Khasi Hills, at about 1,400 m, 69 km from Shillong and 15 km west of Cherrapunji. It is famous for one statistic: with an average of 11,872 mm of rain a year, it is reportedly the wettest place on Earth — though places in Colombia dispute the title.

The numbers are extraordinary. On 17 June 2022 alone, Mawsynram received 1,003.2 mm of rain in 24 hours. Almost all of it falls in the monsoon months, so plan for rain if you come then; the rest of the year is drier. Pair it with a trip to Cherrapunji.

items.title: Rainfall
items.body: About 11,872 mm a year on average

best_time.text: Most of Mawsynram's rain falls in the monsoon months — come then to see the rain at its most dramatic, or in the drier season for easier walking.

places.name: Nohsngithiang (Seven Sisters) Falls
places.summary: A 315 m, seven-stream waterfall near Mawsmai that runs in the rainy season — one of India's tallest.
places.seoDescription: Nohsngithiang, the Seven Sisters Falls near Mawsmai: 315 m and seven streams wide over limestone cliffs, strongest June–September.

images.alt: The seven streams of Nohsngithiang Falls over green cliffs
images.caption: Nohsngithiang (Seven Sisters) Falls

overview.text:
Nohsngithiang Falls — better known as the Seven Sisters or Mawsmai Falls — pours over the limestone cliffs of the Khasi Hills about a kilometre south of Mawsmai village, near Sohra. In full flow it drops 315 metres in seven separate streams spread across about 70 metres of cliff, which makes it one of the tallest waterfalls in India.

The catch is timing: the falls run only in the rainy season. From June to September they are at their most powerful, and the streams stretch most of the way along the cliff; outside the rains you may find only thin threads or bare rock. Late afternoon is the time to be here, when the setting sun lights up the water. Combine it with Mawsmai cave and Nohkalikai Falls on a Sohra day.

places.name: Arwah Cave
places.summary: A limestone cave near Sohra with lit chambers of fossils — shells and fish bones; open 8 am–5 pm.
places.seoDescription: Arwah Cave near Sohra: lit chambers of fossil shells and fish bones among stalactites. Open 8 am–5 pm; bring a torch and sturdy shoes.

images.alt: The entrance to Arwah Cave in the forest near Sohra
images.caption: Arwah Cave

overview.text:
Arwah Cave, or Krem Arwah, is a limestone cave near Sohra that is best known for its fossils. Deeper in, especially towards the end of the cave, lit-up chambers show preserved crustacean shells and fish bones locked in the rock.

On the way you pass stalactites, stalagmites and columns, slide through narrow passages and walk under high ceilings, with streams still running through the rock. Even the path to the entrance is pretty, cut through thick vegetation. It is open from 8 am to 5 pm. Wear sturdy shoes you don't mind getting muddy, take a torch and a light jacket, stay on the marked route and keep flash photography to a minimum to protect the cave.

places.name: Mawmluh Cave
places.summary: A 7.2 km maze cave near Sohra whose stalagmites define the Meghalayan Age; open 9 am–7 pm.
places.seoDescription: Mawmluh Cave near Sohra: a 7.2 km maze cave and IUGS geological heritage site that gave its name to the Meghalayan Age.

overview.text: Mawmluh is a 7.2 km maze cave near Sohra, the fourth longest in the Indian subcontinent. Geologists know it as the place that defines the Meghalayan Age — the latest stage of Earth's history — and it is listed among the first 100 geological heritage sites of the International Union of Geological Sciences. It is open from 9 am to 7 pm.

places.name: David Scott Trail
places.summary: A 16 km walk on a British-era trade route from Mawphlang to Lad Mawphlang, over the Umiam.
places.seoDescription: The 16 km David Scott Trail from Mawphlang to Lad Mawphlang: an old Assam–Bangladesh trade route through Khasi villages, over the Umiam.

overview.text: The David Scott Trail follows a 16 km stretch of an old British-era trade route between Assam and Bangladesh, from Mawphlang to Lad Mawphlang in the East Khasi Hills. It passes pine forest, meadows and Khasi villages, crosses the Umiam River on a reconstructed suspension bridge, and has a campsite at Pine Hill for those who want to stay out overnight.

places.name: Tura
places.summary: The Garo Hills' main town, at the foot of the Nokrek range — base for Nokrek National Park, Tura Peak and the region's waterfalls.
places.seoTitle: Tura, Garo Hills — gateway to Nokrek
places.seoDescription: Tura, centre of the Garo people: base for Nokrek National Park, Tura Peak (872 m) and waterfalls; 220 km from Guwahati, 323 km from Shillong.

images.commons: File:Interior Nave Tura Baptist Church Meghalaya Oct24 A7CR 03784.jpg
images.caption: Tura Baptist Church

overview.text:
Tura is the main town of the Garo Hills, in the far west of Meghalaya, and the cultural and administrative centre of the Garo people. It sits low, at 349 m, in the foothills of the Nokrek range, among small rivers and green valleys, and its climate stays moderate through the year. Garo and English are the main languages.

Tura Peak rises to 872 m on the east side of town, and the hills around hold waterfalls such as Rongbangdare and Pelgadare. Above all, Tura is the gateway to Nokrek National Park, home of the Nokrek Biosphere Reserve. It is 220 km from Guwahati — closer than Shillong, which is 323 km away by bus or shuttle helicopter.

how_to_reach.text: Tura is 220 km from Guwahati. From Shillong, 323 km away, travel by bus or the shuttle helicopter service.

places.name: Nokrek National Park
places.summary: The core of UNESCO's Nokrek Biosphere Reserve near Tura — primates, red pandas and the trek to Nokrek Peak.
places.seoDescription: Nokrek National Park near Tura: core of a UNESCO biosphere reserve, home to seven primate species, red pandas and clouded leopards; base at Daribokgre.

images.alt: Forested ridges of Nokrek National Park
images.caption: Nokrek National Park

overview.text:
Nokrek National Park lies about 2 km from Tura Peak in the Garo Hills and forms the core of the Nokrek Biosphere Reserve, which UNESCO added to its list of biosphere reserves in 2009. Set up in 1986, the park covers about 47 sq km of hill forest, and all the important rivers of the Garo Hills rise in its range.

It is one of Meghalaya's richest areas for wildlife. Seven species of primates live here — the rare stump-tailed macaque is often seen along the main trail to Nokrek Peak — and the park is known for the red panda, the hoolock gibbon and the clouded leopard. Daribokgre, the last village on the northern side, is the usual base camp for visitors and researchers; the quieter southern side is reached via Tura Peak Reserved Forest.

places.name: Siju Cave
places.summary: The Garo Hills' famous bat cave by the Simsang river, home to tens of thousands of bats.
places.seoDescription: Siju Dobakkol, the bat cave of the Garo Hills near Napak Lake and the Simsang: 4,772 m surveyed, home to tens of thousands of bats.

images.commons: File:Entrance Siju Cave South Garo Oct24 A7CR 04109.jpg
images.caption: Siju Cave

overview.text:
Siju Dobakkol — the 'bat cave' — is a limestone cave in the Garo Hills, near Napak Lake and the Simsang river, and it is home to tens of thousands of bats. It is also one of the most thoroughly studied caves in the Indian subcontinent: scientists first explored it in 1922, and it has a rich record of cave-dwelling spiders, crabs and insects.

The cave has been surveyed for 4,772 m, but nearly all of that is filled with water, so ordinary visitors see only the first stretch, with its stalactites and stalagmites. Inside the temperature stays at about 21–26 °C all year. Go with a local guide, wear shoes that can get wet and take a good torch.

overview.text:
Balpakram National Park sits at about 910 m in the South Garo Hills, close to the Bangladesh border, and was inaugurated in December 1987. Its name means "land of the eternal wind" in Garo myth, and the Garo believe the spirits of the dead rest here on their way to the afterlife. It is part of the Garo Hills Conservation Area, which is on UNESCO's tentative World Heritage list.

The landscape mixes subtropical forest, grassland and bamboo, with carnivorous pitcher plants and drosera among the flora. The wildlife list is long — barking deer, wild water buffalo, red panda, Bengal tiger and Indian elephant among them — and its rivers and lakes make it a rewarding place for birdwatchers. It is remote: plan with local guides.
